cards.explanation: The answer is a spirit of animosity. God sent it between Abimelech, who reigned over Israel, and the leaders of Shechem. Animosity is bad blood, the kind of ill will that sours a relationship. It also caused them to treat Abimelech deceitfully (Judges 9:23).

The answer is so justice comes for the seventy sons, and the text says it outright. It was “…in order that the crime against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come to justice…” (Judges 9:24). Jerubbaal is the man also called Gideon (Judges 6:32). Their blood is to be avenged on Abimelech and on the Shechem leaders who helped him.

The answer is False. Abimelech is not the only one. The text says the blood of the seventy sons would be avenged “…on their brother Abimelech and on the leaders of Shechem, who had helped him murder his brothers.” (Judges 9:24). Both are named, friends, and both are going to answer for it.

The answer is that it gets reported to Abimelech. The Shechem leaders ambush from the hilltops and rob everyone passing by, and word of it goes to Abimelech. Now the king knows something is up. The report goes straight to the man the ambush was set against.

The answer is cursed. At the festival they cursed Abimelech, and they did it as they ate and drank in the house of their god. Imagine a festival where the entertainment is cursing the king. Gaal son of Ebed, the newcomer the leaders put their confidence in, is about to speak up too (Judges 9:26, 28). The mood in that room is not friendly to Abimelech.

The answer is remove him. Gaal son of Ebed, a newcomer the Shechem leaders have put their confidence in, claims that if the people were under his authority, he would remove Abimelech. He adds a dare: “Muster your army and come out!” That's a lot of nerve for a man who just arrived.

The answer is True. Zebul, the governor of the city, burned with anger when he heard Gaal, and he covertly sent messengers to Abimelech. The message says Gaal and his brothers have come to Shechem and are stirring up the city against him. Zebul heard it all and didn't sit on it.

The answer is to lie in wait tonight and attack at sunrise. Zebul tells Abimelech and his people to come tonight and lie in wait in the fields. Then at sunrise they are to advance against the city. When Gaal and his men come out, Abimelech is to do to them whatever he is able. Zebul sent that message covertly, so I bet he did not want it read out loud at the gate!

The answer is that the shadows of the mountains look like men to Gaal. Gaal sees people coming down from the mountains, and Zebul, the governor of the city, brushes off what Gaal is pointing at. Then Gaal says it again and points to people coming from the center of the land (Judges 9:36-37).

The answer is fight. Zebul asks, “Where is your gloating now?” and reminds Gaal what he said about Abimelech. Then he tells Gaal to go out now and fight them. Zebul takes Gaal's own words and hands them right back.

The answer is that Gaal flees and many Shechemites fall wounded. Gaal went out and fought, but Abimelech pursued him and Gaal fled. Many Shechemites fell wounded all the way to the entrance of the gate. Gaal said he'd remove Abimelech, and it was Gaal who ran.

The answer is that he lies in wait and attacks them. Abimelech hears the people have gone into the fields, so he takes his men and lies in wait. When he sees the people coming out of the city, he rises up against them and attacks. Once again he sets up an ambush.

The answer is True. Abimelech takes his men and divides them into three companies. The first time, when he set out by night and lay in wait against Shechem, it was four (Judges 9:34). So he's mixing it up this time.

The answer is demolished. After a full day of fighting, Abimelech captured the city and killed its people. Then he demolished it and sowed it with salt. It's a hard thing to read, friends, and I think it's fine to feel that.

The answer is a branch from the trees. Abimelech takes his axe, cuts a branch and lifts it to his shoulder. Then he tells his men, “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” This one is heavy, friends, because the branches are about to be used against the people in the inner chamber.
The answer is False, and the text is clear. Abimelech tells his men, “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” Then each man cuts his own branch and follows him. Nobody stays behind.

The answer is about a thousand men and women. That's the number the text gives. The branches were piled against the inner chamber and set on fire above them, and it kills everyone in the tower of Shechem. This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it deserves a quiet moment.
The answer is True. When Abimelech comes to attack the tower in Thebez, he approaches its entrance to set it on fire. He's right up at the door. That's close, and it matters in the next verse.

The answer is an upper millstone. A woman dropped it on Abimelech's head, and it crushed his skull. That's the top stone of a grinding set. It came down from the roof where the people of Thebez had gone up.

The answer is that he tells his armor-bearer to draw his sword and kill him. Abimelech quickly calls his armor-bearer and says, “Draw your sword and kill me…” The armor-bearer runs his sword through him, and he dies. It's a hard scene, friends, and the text doesn't soften it.

The answer is woman. Abimelech says, “…lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’…” That's the reason he gives for what he asks. It tells us what was on his mind in his last moments, and it's his own reason, not God's.

The answer is that they all go home. When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home. No crowning of a new king, no rebuilding, just heading home. The story of his rule closes quietly.

The answer is Jotham son of Jerubbaal. The text says God brought all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them. That wraps up the story of Abimelech and Shechem, friends, and with it this whole story of Gideon and Abimelech.
